item.title: How does a mother’s touch lead to a scientific breakthrough?
item.description:
The newborn wriggled as she was lowered onto her mother’s chest, minuscule fists clenched, eyes fluttering, chest softly rising and falling. As a nurse wrapped a binding around the pair to steady the tiny body, the baby snuggled into her mother’s skin. The mother began to weep.

“I quickly asked her if she was all right,” says Dr. Sugandha Arya. “The baby had been born 48 hours earlier and immediately taken away to the NICU. She was crying because this was the first time after giving birth that she’d ever touched her baby.”

“She was crying because this was the first time after giving birth that she’d ever touched her baby.”

The proven power of kangaroo mother care

That poignant scene unfolded in a hospital in India during a clinical trial whose findings could help save the lives of 150,000 premature and low-birthweight babies around the world each year.

Across the globe, one in 10 babies is born preterm, meaning before 37 full weeks of pregnancy. Survival rates of preterm babies vary widely. Prematurity can have a stark effect on overall health, significantly increasing the likelihood of major and chronic illness, disability, and developmental delays.

Preterm babies have many needs, according to Dr. Arya, a pediatric specialist at Safdarjung Hospital in Delhi, India, and one of the clinical trial’s onsite investigators. These include infection prevention, early feeding with breast milk, respiratory support, and thermal care.

The practice of kangaroo mother care (KMC) helps address those needs. Named for the way kangaroo mothers carry and nurse their infants in their pouch, KMC involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact between the mother (or a caregiver) and the baby, as well as breastfeeding when possible. KMC keeps babies warm and stable. It’s also adaptable and can happen in conjunction with oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids, and even more intensive respiratory support.

Early research showed that KMC led to a significant reduction in newborn deaths. The intervention has been recommended for years as important for preterm and low-birthweight babies, but only if they are stable at birth or once they have been stabilized, which could take days or even weeks for very preterm and sick newborns.

Bringing immediacy to kangaroo mother care

New findings from the clinical trial, which was conducted at five hospitals in five countries—including Safdarjung Hospital in India—suggest that a variation of KMC could prove to be even more of a lifesaver. The trial ran from December 2017 to January 2020 in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania, with funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation as part of its commitment to help ensure the health of women and their newborns before, during, and after childbirth.

Unstable infants with a birth weight between 1 and 1.799 kilograms were put into one of two groups. One group received immediate KMC, during which the mother or caregiver provided up to 17 hours of skin-to-skin contact per day in a mother-newborn ICU. The other group received conventional care in an incubator or warmer until the baby’s condition stabilized, followed by KMC afterwards.

The clinical trial set out to answer the question of whether KMC could be used for every preterm baby, stable or not, and to compare the benefits of immediate versus standard KMC for all babies, whether stable or not.

“Our question became,” says Dr. Harish Chellani, the head of pediatrics at Safdarjung Hospital and a key investigator in the clinical trial, “Can we save more babies if we keep the mother and baby together?”

“Can we save more babies if we keep the mother and baby together?”

The findings showed a 25% reduction in preterm deaths in the immediate KMC group. The trial was so successful that it was stopped early because everyone involved decided it was unethical to deny other preterm and low-birthweight babies what was clearly lifesaving care.

Using calculations from the trial’s results, a team of trial experts estimated that globally, immediate KMC could save 150,000 more babies every year.

From “standard” to “immediate”

As a result of the clinical trial, the World Health Organization issued new guidelines in November 2022 advising that all preterm and low-birthweight babies have immediate skin-to-skin contact with a caregiver after birth—without any initial time in an incubator, irrespective of the baby’s birth weight, gestational age, or stability.

That marked a significant change from earlier guidance, which called for preterm babies and mothers to be cared for by different departments in separate hospital sections. With immediate KMC, they are kept together in the same area, allowing for continuous skin-to-skin contact and integrated care from an integrated medical team.

“No change comes without challenges,” says Dr. Pratima Mittal, who was involved with the clinical trial when she was the head of the obstetrics department at Safdarjung Hospital. During that time, she oversaw necessary adjustments to the hospital’s physical spaces for women in labor, as well as updates to procedures affecting labor and delivery patients—including infection prevention practices, policies, and personnel.

What made it all work, says Dr. Mittal, was the commitment of hospital leaders as well as good communication and training.

“Strong leadership is very important,” she says. In this case, that meant clear alignment among the heads of the neonatology and obstetrics departments and the medical superintendent.

There was some initial apprehension as the trial began, but Dr. Mittal found that the positive results soon became a strong motivating factor. Now that the trial has concluded, the motivation is even stronger. “The existing evidence is very, very robust,” she says. “We can depend on it.”

“The existing evidence is very, very robust. We can depend on it.”

Shifting the paradigm of care

Dr. Nitya Wadhwa also notes the importance of evidence. A senior professor at the Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, she supported trial protocols, guidelines, research, and data at the trial site in India. She says the neonatal nurses involved in the trial were initially apprehensive and “talked about how much extra work this would be.” But as the trial progressed, their apprehensions vanished. Immediate KMC did not translate into more work for them—quite the opposite, since mothers and caregivers were now more involved in the babies’ care. And the positive results were extremely motivating.

Dr. Wadhwa also notes the significance of getting extended families and caregivers involved. “We saw whole families coming in with the mother for delivery,” she says. “And so we had surrogates who could provide the skin-to-skin contact, whether a sister or grandmother.” Further, she saw mothers who had experienced immediate KMC become KMC champions, encouraging other new mothers and families. “It was very heartening,” she says.

That aligns with what Aarti Kumar has seen in her decades of work in newborn care and KMC. As the CEO of the Community Empowerment Lab in Uttar Pradesh, India, Kumar helped lead a study of standard KMC in 2004 (also funded by the Gates Foundation) and has been a passionate advocate ever since.

Mothers regularly tell Kumar, “The baby doesn’t startle and is sleeping better. I have more breast milk, earlier.” These positive experiences directly correlate with the likelihood that mothers will continue KMC once they get home, she says.

A few years ago, Kumar led an immediate KMC workshop for nurses. She first had them express their concerns and resistance, and then she shared empirical and anecdotal evidence. She asked these frontline health workers to imagine immediate KMC from the perspective of a newborn that has just come into the world, leaving the womb that kept it safe and nourished.

To Kumar’s astonishment, “many nurses cried during this exercise,” she says. “They had a deep sense of realization that the baby needs to be reunited with its mother.” Some nurses told Kumar that the workshop shifted the way they thought about the babies, especially those with little chance of survival. “That was a transformative moment,” she says.

Moving toward a new standard of care

“The bottom line is that skin-to-skin contact should be started as early as possible and continue as long as possible,” says Dr. Wadhwa.

Many hospitals and clinics already implement standard KMC, but a large percentage need updates to their facilities, as well as staff training to embrace and offer immediate KMC. Those updates include redesigned health systems in the form of mother-newborn ICUs that provide care and medical treatment for both mother and newborn with no separation time or distance between them—even if the baby needs additional medical support.

“The bottom line is that skin-to-skin contact should be started as early as possible and continue as long as possible.”

In this new environment, medical staff involve mothers and caregivers in clinical care. What’s more, mothers and caregivers have dignified spaces for cleaning and bathing, are provided nutritious meals, and are heard and supported. Visitor policies also need updating to enhance the participation of caregivers and family members so immediate KMC is a shared responsibility.

Above all, Dr. Arya believes that what’s needed is space in people’s minds. “We need to make ourselves open to change. If you change a mindset, you’ll be able to find answers to all obstacles,” she says.

item.title: Come to work with an obstetrician in Kano, Nigeria
item.description:
Pregnancy should always be safe, but in Nigeria some families are scared about what the outcome might be. About 75,000 women in my country die each year during pregnancy or delivery—about a quarter of them from postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), or severe blood loss after giving birth. As their doctor, you are watching their life slip out of your hands.

The most tragic part of this is that many maternal deaths are preventable. But I know that progress is possible, with smart interventions and dedicated health care workers. I see it every day in my work, and it’s what drives me to wake up every morning and do what I do.

Come spend a day with me in Kano, Nigeria, and see how we are working to make every birth a joyful one.

How Dr. Galadanci starts her day

I start my day at 5:30 with the dawn prayer, then rest a little more and get up around 7 to get ready for work. I have breakfast with my family and begin answering messages and calls on the way to work.

To be honest, it wasn’t obvious that I would be able to pursue 7-year-old Hadiza’s dream of being a doctor. My father was an educator, and he wanted all of his children, including girls, to be educated, but that was not the norm at the time. When I received my bachelor’s in medicine and surgery from Ahmadu Bello University in Zaria, I became the first female obstetrician trained in the Kano region. I practiced for many years, but I wondered, with all the interventions that exist, why are Nigerian women still dying at rates far higher than in other countries? As much as I loved working with patients, I decided to also become a researcher so I could affect policy and save many more lives.

Going from being a clinician to also a researcher gives you an advantage because you are intimately familiar with the problems that clinicians face, Dr. Galadanci says.

Improving health outcomes for women in Kano

At our hospital, one of the biggest obstacles to addressing PPH is the failure to diagnose in time. PPH is defined as losing 500 milliliters of blood in the first 24 hours after giving birth. Health care providers usually estimate the amount of blood loss based on a visual assessment, which is very hard to do accurately.

I cared for my cousin during her fourth pregnancy. Everything was fine leading up to the birth, but when she came in to deliver, her blood pressure spiked. After she delivered, there was blood everywhere. I administered every single treatment I could think of—tranexamic acid, misoprostol, oxytocin—but she continued to bleed. I knew I had to do something, so we rushed her to the operating room for a hysterectomy and gave her six pints of blood. She stabilized by morning.

My colleagues and I at the hospital eventually introduced the PPH drape, an inexpensive plastic sheet that channels a mother’s blood into a V-shaped plastic bag with measurement markings so health workers can see and track blood loss in real time.

This plastic drape, which costs less than US$2, helps quickly and accurately identify postpartum hemorrhage.

Being able to diagnose PPH early is the first step in a protocol known as E-MOTIVE. E stands for early detection—using the PPH drape. Each subsequent letter indicates a step in the process—uterine massage, oxytocic drugs, tranexamic acid, intravenous fluids, examination, and escalation—but in reality, the idea is to do them all as quickly as possible without waiting because time is the most critical factor in stopping the bleeding. Before E-MOTIVE, clinicians would typically administer one intervention, wait to see if it worked, and, if not, try another, losing valuable time. Waiting can cost lives.

What is beautiful about E-MOTIVE is that it doesn’t require additional clinical training, because these are mostly standard interventions, just bundled together so as not to lose time.

With support from the Gates Foundation, researchers in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, and Tanzania, including my team, conducted a study on the effectiveness of E-MOTIVE involving 210,132 patients who had vaginal deliveries. Our results, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023, showed a 60% reduction in heavy bleeding in the intervention group compared with patients who received usual care. Within 6 months, the World Health Organization adopted E-MOTIVE in its guidelines. Countries have implemented it, too—including Nigeria, thanks to partnerships with the Federal Ministry of Health & Social Welfare and the state ministries of health.

Frontline health care workers have told me that since they started using E-MOTIVE, they haven’t had a single mother die from PPH. If we could implement it across Nigeria, this approach has the potential to significantly reduce deaths from PPH.

I know we can do even more. I want to address preeclampsia, another leading reason moms die in birth. I am optimistic about the future because we have many new tools to improve maternal and child health. Simple sensors can monitor high blood pressure, a symptom of preeclampsia. Ultrasound devices that use artificial intelligence can help health care providers in rural settings refer high-risk patients to the right care. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machines can enable premature babies to breathe more effectively. I’ve seen E-MOTIVE adopted in record time, so that gives me hope that these other innovations can move quickly from research to policy—and save lives.

Dr. Hadiza Galadanci is a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University and an OB-GYN and researcher at Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital in Kano, Nigeria. An advocate for maternal health in Nigeria and globally, Dr. Galadanci is the director of the Africa Center of Excellence for Population Health and Policy. 

About Maternal & Child Health

Thanks to global focus, coordination, and effort, child mortality has been cut in half since 2000. But thousands of mothers and children are still dying from preventable causes during pregnancy and childbirth.

At the foundation, we are working to make these preventable deaths a thing of the past and give every mother and child worldwide a chance to thrive.

item.title: How will global health innovations shape tomorrow? Take the quiz
item.description:
What does a child born today have to look forward to as they grow up? In global health, a number of lifesaving innovations are making the future feel more hopeful.

New vaccines to save more babies’ lives. Better health care for moms and newborns. Smarter ways to prevent disease. These are all part of a global vision, shared by many, to improve the lives of mothers and children for generations to come. Here’s the catch: Realizing that vision depends on investments the world makes today.

The good news is, the world has already proven that progress is possible. Since 2000, child deaths have been cut in half. Maternal mortality has declined by 40%. All because health care workers, researchers, nonprofits, companies, and governments have made big bets on innovation.

But what comes next? The innovations emerging now—some simple, some surprising—could play a huge role in shaping the future of health care, improving and saving even more lives over the next 20 years.

Take the health care quiz below to explore how innovations in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment can work together to advance progress in global health.

So what do we think the next 20 years will bring? The future of health care isn’t set, but the innovations we just explored offer a glimpse of what’s possible: Communities around the world that are healthier and more resilient. Healthy moms who give birth to healthy babies, no matter where they live. And the next generation growing up without fear of deadly infectious diseases.

item.title: Helping every child reach their full potential—no matter where they’re born
item.description:
In 2023, nearly 5 million children died before their 5th birthday—most of them from causes like malnutrition and preventable diseases.

Kids in the poorest parts of the world are 80 times more likely to die before age 5 than those in the wealthiest countries.

At the Gates Foundation, we believe that every child, no matter where they are from, deserves the chance to thrive and live out their dreams.

That’s why we work with partners to improve the health and well-being of children all over the world.

We start by helping mothers.

Every year, about 260,000 women—more than 90% of them in low- and middle-income countries—die from pregnancy- or childbirth-related complications.

To help protect mothers, we support the development of new health care tools.

For example, two-thirds of the world’s people lack access to diagnostic imaging, including ultrasounds. We work with partners to get portable ultrasound devices powered by artificial intelligence that pair with mobile phones into remote areas so midwives and nurses can help mothers have healthier pregnancies.

Even relatively simple interventions can be lifesaving for mothers.

Take the postpartum hemorrhage drape, a V-shaped plastic bag placed under a mother during childbirth that measures blood loss after delivery.

To excel in school and in life, every child needs to learn foundational skills like reading and math.

We also work with countries to support efforts to improve their digital public infrastructure, including systems like digital payments that connect people to services, markets, and each other.

Just as roads and railways were essential to prosperity in earlier eras, inclusive and thoughtfully implemented digital systems can play a role in strengthening economies and expanding opportunity for all.

Digital public infrastructure is key to making progress on many of the issues we work on…. The future is digital. Let’s make sure it’s a future that benefits everyone.

We believe in a few fundamental truths:

Every person deserves the chance to live a healthy, productive life.

Every child deserves the opportunity to pursue their dreams.

Anyone, no matter where they’re from, can change their community and the world for the better.

Since our foundation began its work 26 years ago, child mortality worldwide has fallen by half.

That means 5 million more kids every year who are staying alive.

In 2026, we are continuing to focus on improving the health of mothers and babies, fighting infectious diseases, and expanding economic opportunity so every child can reach their full potential.

item.title: Three takeaways from the 2025 Goalkeepers Report
item.description:
In 2025, for the first time in a generation, the number of children who die before they turn 5 is projected to rise, to 4.8 million. The death of a child is always a tragedy, but it is all the more heartbreaking when the cause is a preventable disease.

We know what it takes to ensure that more children live to blow out the candles on their 5th birthday cake. The 2025 Goalkeepers Report provides a roadmap for saving more children’s lives, combining smart spending with innovation. The world already has the tools to prevent the vast majority of child deaths, and with even more promising breakthroughs on the horizon, we could end some life-threatening diseases for good.

Here are three things you need to know from this year’s Goalkeepers Report:

1. Primary health care is the smartest investment we can make in children’s health.

The most effective tool for saving children’s lives is also the most basic: primary health care. For less than US$100 per person per year, a robust primary health care system can prevent up to 90% of child deaths. These systems are the foundation for keeping people healthy, and they achieve extraordinary results with modest investments.

Strong primary health care systems help ensure that mothers deliver babies safely, children get vaccines on time, and diseases are caught before they can worsen or spread. Countries can get an incredible return on their health investments when they commit to building this foundation.

In Nigeria’s Gombe State, at a time when the health system received only 3.5% of the state’s already limited budget, the government focused on turning around its primary health care system.

Without any outside resources, it renovated or built primary health centers in every one of the state’s 114 wards, or counties. Gombe State showed that by focusing on the basics and making smart investments in technology, more people could gain access to care to keep them healthy.

2. Innovation allows every dollar to go further when it comes to saving children’s lives.

We live in a time of extraordinary innovation—and we must apply that innovation to get the most from every dollar spent to save lives. For example, across sub-Saharan Africa, which has hundreds of millions of malaria cases each year, data and technology are significantly boosting efforts to combat this potentially deadly disease.

In Zambia, teams of individuals who spray insecticide in the highest-risk areas are relying on a digital “smart maps” to guide their work, reducing costs by over 20% per case of malaria prevented. These savings are reinvested in additional interventions, protecting more children and families from the disease.

Similarly, innovation in vaccine formulations allows countries to deliver the same protection against certain diseases using fewer doses, saving billions of dollars. Health workers used to give three doses of the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) to protect against pneumonia, the biggest infectious killer of children under age 5. But recently the World Health Organization determined that one primary dose plus one booster is just as effective.

If countries with established PCV programs adopt this new schedule, it could save US$2 billion by 2050. That’s money that can go toward protecting even more children from preventable diseases.

3. New scientific breakthroughs could end certain diseases once and for all.

Nearly half of all child deaths occur in the first month of life, before babies are old enough to be immunized. Starting in the late 2000s, scientists began working on maternal vaccines that enable a pregnant woman to pass on antibodies to her baby through the placenta—like the vaccines now widely used to prevent tetanus and pertussis.

These vaccines can help address some of the deadliest viruses and bacteria that threaten newborns in low-income countries. A maternal vaccine is in development for Group B streptococcus, an often asymptomatic disease that can cause blood infections, brain damage, and even death within hours of a child being born. Another vaccine, for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the leading cause of infant pneumonia, is in use in several high-income countries. It is now being rolled out in low-income countries, where the majority of RSV deaths occur, potentially saving millions of lives.

Scientists like Ugandan entomologist Krystal Mwesiga Birungi, who grew up watching her brother suffer unbearable fevers during repeated bouts of malaria, are studying how to reduce the number of malaria-transmitting mosquitos or prevent them from carrying malaria altogether, using novel genetic technologies. While millions of lives have been saved through widespread use of mosquito nets, insecticide spraying, medications, and vaccines, none of these interventions has been able to stop the disease from claiming hundreds of thousands of lives a year. But novel genetic approaches may hold the promise to do this, potentially eliminating the disease for good by 2040.

The 2025 Goalkeepers report makes one thing clear: We know how to protect children from preventable diseases, and we’ve made a great deal of progress. We’re getting closer. But that isn’t good enough. Every mother deserves prenatal care that will support her and her baby in having a healthy birth. Every infant deserves to enter the world free of the diseases we know how to prevent. And every parent should be able to watch their child celebrate their 5th birthday. Our generation has the knowledge and the tools to ensure that everyone, everywhere, can live a healthy life and thrive.

Even in the face of mounting challenges, we can do a lot more by making the right investments. But only if we choose to.

QUIZ: How is climate change affecting what we eat?
item.description:
What’s on your dinner plate?

Maybe it’s a grain, like wheat or sorghum. Or a legume, like soybeans or chickpeas. Whatever your favorite food, on this Earth Day it’s worth asking: How is a changing climate affecting what goes on our plates?

How farmers are adapting to extreme weather

This shift is already happening in regions long vulnerable to weather extremes, including South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. In Malawi, for example, prolonged drought led to major maize losses in 2024. In India, extreme heat has shriveled wheat crops in recent years. And in Pakistan, torrential flooding has wiped out large areas of farmland.

Events like these have impact far beyond the dinner table. Across these regions, many families depend on the land for both their food and their livelihood. Smallholder farmers—many of them women—do the vital work to feed their families and communities. When crops fail, communities experience more hunger and fewer opportunities for a healthy, stable, and prosperous future.

But something else is happening, too. Smallholder farmers are changing what they grow, how they grow it, and how they prepare for an uncertain future.

They’re adopting innovations like: improved seed varieties bred to withstand heat, simple irrigation methods that can help keep crops alive during drought, and planting ancient, climate-resilient grains. And with advisory services powered by artificial intelligence available on their phones, they’re tapping into new sources of information that help them identify plant diseases and respond to extreme weather before it reaches their farms.

Smallholder farmers like Phoebe Mwangangi in Kenya are adopting innovative farming techniques such as rainwater harvesting and minimal soil disturbance and planting climate-resilient crops to adapt to climate change and protect their livelihoods.

This kind of progress matters.

Decades of evidence show that when a farmer has the tools to adapt to a changing climate, she can better feed her family and protect her livelihood. Health improves. Yields increase. Surplus can be sold at the market. And with more stable income comes the ability to invest in education, nutrition, and the future.

So what does this mean for the foods we rely on every day? Which ones are more resilient in a changing climate—and why?

Take our quiz to explore how different foods are grown, how they’re being affected by climate change, and what exciting innovations farmers are using to adapt.

Smallholder farmers on the front lines are adapting to the changing climate by adopting innovations that make their crops more productive, drought tolerant, and disease resistant. That’s a win for smallholder farmers, for the families that rely on the food they produce, and for local economies. 

About Economic Opportunity

Everyone deserves the chance to live a healthy, productive life—and have access to the tools and resources to shape their own future. But for many people—especially women and girls—access to basic needs like nutritious food, quality education, and jobs is still out of reach. That’s why we’re focusing on areas with the greatest potential to improve lives, like agriculture and education.

item.title: Teaching kids in their national languages is transforming classrooms in Senegal
item.description:
Seven-year-old Mansour Fall grips his pen tightly as he copies notes from the chalkboard. For such a small boy, he has big dreams. “I want to be president,” he says.

His mother, Aminata Ba, knows that in Senegal, education—in French, the country’s official language—has long been viewed as the path to achieving that kind of dream.

But that path is beginning to change.

In Senegal’s schools, students have traditionally been taught in French even though less than 1% of the country’s population speaks it at home. Like roughly 80% of Senegalese, Ba is more comfortable speaking Wolof, one of the 25 national languages in Senegal. But when she was growing up, chatting in Wolof was “strictly forbidden in the classroom,” she recalls.

Senegal’s Ministry of Education began rolling out a bilingual education program in Wolof and French in 2015, gradually expanding it across the country. By the time it reached Mansour’s classroom, Ba was hesitant. Not having learned to read or write in her national languages, she already feared she wouldn’t be able to help Mansour study. And now, how would he become president without being fluent in French?

Her doubts didn’t last long.

When Ba saw how learning in both languages helped Mansour grasp new concepts and grow more confident in class, she reconsidered. “I changed my mind once I saw how much my son was thriving in class, how focused he was, and how good his grades were,” she says.

The science behind bilingual learning

For decades, Senegalese students were taught exclusively in French even though most of them spoke a different language at home. Research shows that this makes it harder for them to gain early literacy skills. Before the bilingual approach was introduced by the Ministry of Education in partnership with the nonprofit organization Associates in Research and Education for Development (ARED), a Gates Foundation grantee, many young learners struggled to grasp foundational concepts.

In 2025, ARED was awarded the Yidan Prize—one of the world’s most prestigious honors in education—for its work advancing instruction in national languages.

“Over 70% of children couldn’t even read a simple sentence,” says Mamadou Amadou Ly, executive director of ARED.

Senegal’s bilingual education model for primary school students is beginning to change that. By gaining foundational skills in both Wolof and French, students are not only reading earlier and participating more confidently in class, but they are far more likely to complete school—and become higher earners as adults. The bilingual model, known as MOHEBS—Modèle Harmonisé d’Enseignement Bilingue au Sénégal, or Unified Framework for Bilingual Education in Senegal— is also serving as an example for other countries.

Turning a literacy program into a national strategy

For 15 years, ARED helped adults achieve literacy by teaching in Senegal’s several national languages. Ly believed the same approach could work in primary schools. “We asked ourselves, Why not bring our expertise in national languages into formal education?” he recalls.  

Earlier efforts to introduce bilingual learning in the 1970s stalled, largely because the country lacked a unified national strategy. When Ly approached the Ministry of Education, officials were in the middle of rolling out a new competency-based curriculum, and they were reluctant to take on another reform.

ARED then proposed a compromise: a pilot program providing free afternoon sessions. The results were striking. “We proved that children learned better with just those afternoon sessions, and it even improved their behavior and learning during the regular school day,” says Ly. “Parents noticed it, too.”

Soon, parents and school inspectors asked for the program to become part of the official school schedule.

When evidence becomes policy

One assessment showed that for students taught in national languages, there was an overall 29 percentage point increase in the proportion of students meeting the program’s oral reading and reading comprehension benchmark than those of their monolingually educated peers. Those results helped pave the way for MOHEBS.

Today, MOHEBS is available in 13 of Senegal’s 16 education regions and in six national languages, with two more to be added in 2026. Having overcome early hesitation from parents and teachers, the next challenge is expansion. “Our big challenge is developing teaching materials,” says Ndeye Aby Ndao Cissé, the director of elementary education in the Ministry of Education.

For Cissé, the investment goes far beyond the classroom. “This isn’t just an investment in childhood—the child who succeeds today becomes tomorrow’s adult,” she says. Human capital is central to Senegal’s Agenda 2050, the country’s long-term development vision. “With our harmonized bilingual model, we’re shaping responsible Senegalese citizens who will drive the country’s social and economic progress.”

What changed inside the classroom

item.title: When we invest in women, everyone gains
item.description:
When women have the power to make decisions about their lives—and access to the tools and resources they need—economies grow, families are healthier, and communities are more resilient. Closing gender gaps in health, entrepreneurship, and economic participation could add trillions to the global economy—yet nearly every woman in the world faces barriers that limit her potential.

I’ve seen how investment in women changes outcomes—in the data as well as in my own professional life.

Early in my career, I looked up to one of the senior leaders at the company. Her magnetic leadership inspired me—I knew I wanted her in my corner. In our early conversations, she taught me the difference between a mentor and a sponsor. A mentor offers guidance, and a sponsor advocates for you when you’re not in the room.

She became my sponsor at key moments in my career, advocating for my work, positioning me for opportunities, and ensuring that my contributions were seen. I worked hard and earned my accomplishments, but she helped open doors for me that might otherwise have remained closed. To this day, I think of her as part of my personal board of directors, a practice I have brought into my personal career management philosophy.

As we mark International Women’s Day and reflect on this year’s theme, “Give to Gain,” I’m reminded that what this leader did wasn’t just generous to me personally—it was an investment. When we invest in women—by expanding their access to education, health care, capital, or mentorship—those gains ripple outward.

The economic development barriers women still face

Despite how much progress is possible, too many barriers still prevent women from achieving their true potential. Women spend, on average, 2.4 more hours per day on unpaid care work than men. And an astonishing 96% of the world’s women live in countries where they do not have full legal equality with men. Globally, women earn just 61 cents for every dollar men earn. Once child care access and personal safety are factored in, there isn’t a single country in the world where women have genuine full equality.

These barriers don’t just hold women back—they result in families, communities, and countries missing out on the ripple effects of women’s full participation in society. 

“Giving to gain” isn’t an abstract idea. It shows up in individual lives in powerful ways. Carol Welch, director of economic opportunity in the foundation’s India office, recalls how an early supervisor invested in her: 

My first boss put me in the driver’s seat before I felt ready. She encouraged me to speak up in meetings with senior U.S. Treasury and International Monetary Fund officials—she told me it meant I was raising the right issues.

That vote of confidence gave me the courage to keep going.

Now I try to do the same for others—creating space for women to step forward, build skills, and lead. When we’re working to change entrenched systems, we need the best talent. That means investing in women.

Smart investments in women that unlock change

Smart investments are an important part of giving to gain. The foundation’s long-term investments target structural barriers to women’s equality and economic development, helping to change systems so women can thrive. For example, women make up the majority of smallholder farmers in Africa, and training them to use climate-smart agriculture techniques means they are better able to feed their families and communities, invest in their children’s health and education, and spread their knowledge by training others in the same techniques. 

Agriculture is only one piece of the puzzle. Too many women are excluded from the formal economy. Expanding financial inclusion through digital financial services gives women access to capital, secure ways to transact and save, and the tools to start and expand businesses.

Health care is another area that needs investment. Many women can’t access essential health services or obtain the contraceptives they want to use. Strengthening primary health care systems and expanding access to contraception enables women to make informed choices about their families and their futures.

Together, these investments in women can be transformative. Not only can they help women realize their aspirations, but their effects can ripple out through their communities and their countries. When women can participate fully in the economy, they have money to spend in their neighborhoods, they can send their children to school, and they can share valuable new ideas and insights that the world can benefit from. And the data shows that these investments pay off.

Effects that extend far beyond individual women

By supporting more economic opportunity for women, policymakers could boost global GDP by more than 7% by 2030. Just by closing the gender health gap, the global economy could grow by US$1 trillion—every single year—because investing in women’s health enables them to attend school and work and provide for their families. And closing the entrepreneurship gap by enabling women to start and expand businesses at the same rate as men could boost the global economy by an estimated US$5 trillion to US$6 trillion. Tapping into women’s talents and energy unleashes economic growth that benefits everyone. We can’t afford to miss out on these gains.

The multiplier effect of investing in women is visible at our foundation. Program Officer Ashley Jackson recalls how a mentor here gave her a vote of confidence that changed her trajectory.

Five years ago, I had the privilege of collaborating on a project with a women’s health leader I deeply admire. When the project ended and she encouraged me to apply for the leadership role she was leaving, I was stunned—I didn’t feel ready.

This leader saw something in me that I couldn’t yet see in myself. Her belief in me gave me the courage to step forward before I felt 100% prepared. She showed me that there is more to leadership than tenure—it’s about vision, values, and bringing others along.

Now I try to pay the support forward by naming the strengths I see in women around me—especially when they do not yet see those strengths in themselves—and advocating for them as they pursue new opportunities.

Investing in women builds a better world

I’m inspired by the progress that’s already been made. Between 1970 and 2022, countries around the world adopted more than 2,000 laws that have brought women closer to legal parity with men in their economies. In those decades, countless women have started businesses, made brilliant scientific discoveries, and brought home income that has improved their lives and those of their families.

But progress doesn’t happen by chance. Laws must be implemented and enforced—not just recorded on paper. Opportunities must be intentionally expanded. We know that equal access to loans, health care, education, and well-paying jobs won’t just happen by accident—decision-makers must make it an explicit priority.

There is no version of global progress that does not include women having a seat at the table. When we invest in women, we unlock talent, innovation, and leadership potential that the world cannot afford to leave behind.

About Economic Opportunity

Everyone deserves the chance to live a healthy, productive life—and have access to the tools and resources to shape their own future. But for many people—especially women and girls—access to basic needs like nutritious food, quality education, and jobs is still out of reach. That’s why we’re focusing on areas with the greatest potential to improve lives, like agriculture and education.
